title: Your Laugh Is a 15-Million-Year-Old Secret Code!
summary: Have you ever laughed so hard you couldn't stop? That giggle might be way older than you think! Scientists just discovered that the rhythm of human laughter has stayed almost the same for 15 million years. That's before humans even existed! Researchers at the University of Warwick listened to laughter from four orangutans, two gorillas, three bonobos, four chimpanzees, and four humans. They studied 140 different laugh sounds. And guess what? Every single species laughed with the same steady beat—like a drum keeping time. Dr. Chiara De Gregorio, one of the scientists, said, "We've found a 15-million-year-old clue in an unexpected place: our laughter." She explained that speech doesn't leave fossils, so laughter is a rare window into how talking evolved. But here's the twist: human laughter got faster and more flexible over time. We can change our laugh depending on how we feel—a tickle laugh sounds different from a nervous giggle or a polite chuckle. Other apes can't do that as well. This ability to control our voice, even in laughter, might have been a key step toward speaking. So next time you crack up, remember: you're using an ancient superpower that helped your ancestors learn to talk!
why_it_matters: When you laugh with your friends, you're using an ancient tool that helped our ancestors bond and eventually learn to talk.

background_read: All great apes, including humans, evolved from a common ancestor that lived about 15 million years ago.
Scientists at the University of Warwick (a university in England) have been studying animal sounds to understand how speech developed.
Dr. Chiara De Gregorio (an expert in animal behavior) believes laughter is a key piece of this puzzle.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists from the University of Warwick, including Dr. Chiara De Gregorio.
WHAT: They found that the rhythm of laughter is similar across humans and great apes and has barely changed for 15 million years.
WHERE: The research was done at the University of Warwick in the United Kingdom, using recordings of laughter from apes and humans.
WHY: They wanted to find out how the ability to speak could have evolved, since laughter is a sound we make naturally.

perspectives.description: They see this as a breakthrough that links laughter to the start of spoken language.
They might be happy to learn that our giggles connect us with gorillas and chimpanzees.
Some people might think it's just a fun fact, but it actually helps explain why laughing feels so automatic.
